title: Allocation-size overflow and defensive allocation patterns (CodeSaathi extension)
learningObjectives: Explain why size_t arithmetic can wrap and why checking a product after multiplication is too late.
Use SIZE_MAX and division to prove an element-count multiplication is representable.
Validate multiplication and addition for matrix, flexible-array and header-plus-payload sizes.
Define a predictable policy for zero-sized requests and allocation failure.
Use sizeof *pointer and checked helpers to reduce type-size mistakes.
Test arithmetic boundaries without huge allocations and distinguish representability from memory availability.

understand.concept: Allocation functions accept a byte count of type size_t. Before allocating count elements, code often calculates count multiplied by element_size. Since size_t is unsigned, arithmetic can wrap modulo one more than its maximum value. The product can become a much smaller byte count while the program still believes it allocated space for the original element count.
understand.whyItMatters: If indexing follows the original count after the byte-size calculation wrapped, writes can exceed the allocated object. malloc may succeed for the undersized request, so checking only for a NULL result does not detect the arithmetic defect.
understand.analogy: Treat each function and allocation request as a contract with valid inputs, promised results and defined failure behaviour.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's rules for object lifetime, bounds, arithmetic or library contracts.

explain.narrative: For nonzero element_size, count greater than SIZE_MAX divided by element_size means the product cannot fit in size_t. Reject before evaluating the product. malloc(0) has implementation-defined allocation behaviour; define a policy such as returning NULL for zero elements. Before header_size plus payload_size, verify payload_size is not greater than SIZE_MAX minus header_size. For a flat matrix, validate rows times columns, then element count times element size. Check each operation before evaluation. A representable request may still fail because memory is unavailable, so check malloc separately. Prefer sizeof *items to repeating the pointed-to type.

examples.explanation: The helper defines a zero-size policy and proves the multiplication fits before evaluating it. malloc can still fail, so the caller checks the returned pointer.

examples.title: Check a flexible-array header and payload
examples.explanation: The code checks multiplication before calculating payload, then checks addition before calculating total. Allocation failure is checked separately.

practise.guidedTask: Explain why SIZE_MAX / sizeof(int) plus one must be rejected before multiplication. Implement a helper that returns a status and safe byte count.
practise.independentTask: Explain why SIZE_MAX / sizeof(int) plus one must be rejected before multiplication. Implement a helper that returns a status and safe byte count. Add boundary and failure tests and explain the expected result for each.
hints: Validate inputs before dereferencing or indexing.
Check library return values and document failure behaviour.
Keep output parameters unchanged on failure when promised by the contract.
Release each acquired resource exactly once.
Test normal, boundary and failure paths.
A diagnostic or check proves only what its defined scope covers.

questions.prompt: Why is checking the product after multiplication unsafe?
options: The multiplication may already have wrapped to a smaller size.
questions.answer: The multiplication may already have wrapped to a smaller size.
questions.explanation: Unsigned size arithmetic can wrap; prove the product fits before evaluating it.

questions.prompt: For nonzero element_size, which condition detects overflow?
questions.explanation: The quotient gives the largest count whose product can fit in size_t.

questions.prompt: How should header plus payload be checked?
options: Check payload > SIZE_MAX - header before adding.
questions.answer: Check payload > SIZE_MAX - header before adding.
questions.explanation: SIZE_MAX minus the header is the largest safe additional payload.

questions.prompt: What does a successful overflow check guarantee?
options: The byte count is representable, but allocation may still fail.
questions.answer: The byte count is representable, but allocation may still fail.
questions.explanation: Arithmetic safety and allocation availability are separate.

questions.prompt: Why define a policy for count == 0?
options: To avoid treating malloc(0)'s implementation-dependent result as usable element storage.
Because free cannot accept allocated pointers.
questions.answer: To avoid treating malloc(0)'s implementation-dependent result as usable element storage.
questions.explanation: A documented zero-size policy gives callers predictable semantics.
